This is tricky legal territory here. I'll give you my understanding.

(1) The order stops any further actions to certify anything until after the court hearing.

(2) The US Constitution gives the state legislature the power to choose electors. They have delegated that power, to a certain extent, by having the Sec. of State certify results. However, they still have the power. They can take that delegation away. If they find that the SoS acted in violation of law, or based on fraudulent election results (and SoS was involved in an unconstitutional act regarding the counting of votes), then the legislature can overrule the SoS. It is not the SoS's power. It is the legislature's power. This is something that Atty Ellis brought up today.

(3) If the court (likely going to SCOTUS) determines that the SoS violated the law in performing the certification, then that certification is null and void. At that point, the state legislature will decide what to do.

(4) If the court/SCOTUS determines that certain ballots were illegal and must be nullified, then it will have the same effect.
